displayQuote: Politics have no relation to morals

meta.title: Who really said "Politics have no relation to morals"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Machiavelli everywhere, sourced nowhere. Wikiquote files it as misattributed, origin unclear. The word appears nowhere in Machiavelli's own chapters in Marriott's 1908 translation of The Prince.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Politics have no relation to morals'?
meta.ogDescription: Machiavelli never wrote this line. Wikiquote files it as misattributed, origin unclear. Here is the passage in The Prince it is usually standing in for.

answer.label: Not Machiavelli's words — no source has ever been identified
answer.authorDates: 1469–1527 · Florentine secretary, diplomat and political theorist
answer.sourceLine: No work of Machiavelli’s has been shown to contain this sentence. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗, noting only that it “originates from an unclear source” — and the words moral and morals do not appear anywhere in the body of W. K. Marriott’s 1908 translation of The Prince. The thought is defensibly his: Chapter XV argues that a ruler must “know how to do wrong.” The eight-word slogan itself has no identified source — no first printing, letter or translation has ever been produced for it.

source.heading: The passage it usually stands in for

docMeta.dt: Nearest passage in the credited work

docMeta.dd: W. K. Marriott, 1908 (J. M. Dent & Sons, London)
Discourses on Livy, Book III, Chapter XLI (trans. Ninian Hill Thomson)

source.excerpt:
But, it being my intention to write a thing which shall be useful to him who apprehends it, it appears to me more appropriate to follow up the real truth of the matter than the imagination of it; for many have pictured republics and principalities which in fact have never been known or seen, because how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation; for a man who wishes to act entirely up to his professions of virtue soon meets with what destroys him among so much that is evil.

Hence it is necessary for a prince wishing to hold his own to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity.
trail: Wikiquote’s Machiavelli page ↗ lists the line in its “Misattributed” section, with the whole of its annotation being that it “originates from an unclear source.” No earliest printing is offered, and Quote Investigator has no entry on it.

Searching the complete text of Marriott’s 1908 translation of The Prince ↗ returns four hits for “moral” — all four inside the translator’s introduction. Machiavelli’s own chapters use the word not once, in any form.

Ninian Hill Thomson’s translation of the Discourses on Livy ↗ uses “morals” exactly once, of the Roman censors as “the arbiters of morals in Rome.” Its Book III, Chapter XLI is the nearest passage in substance — closer than anything in The Prince: when a country’s survival is at stake, “no consideration of what is just or unjust, merciful or cruel, praiseworthy or shameful, must intervene.”
Wikisource reproduces the Marriott edition with its title page ↗: published by J. M. Dent & Sons, London and Toronto, and E. P. Dutton & Co., New York, in 1908.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage the slogan is usually standing in for — and the difference is instructive. Machiavelli does not say politics and morals are unrelated; he says a ruler who acts “entirely up to his professions of virtue” among people who do not will be destroyed, so he must know how to do wrong “according to necessity.” The moral vocabulary is still doing work. The slogan throws it out.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the sentence itself, because no source for it has ever been identified — a wording with no known first publication has no determinable copyright history. The genuine texts quoted on this page are a different matter: Marriott’s 1908 translation of The Prince ↗ and Thomson’s translation of the Discourses ↗ are both distributed by Project Gutenberg as public domain in the United States.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.heading: Who was Machiavelli?
author.metaLine: 1469–1527 · Florentine diplomat, historian and political theorist
author.bio: Machiavelli spent fourteen years as second chancellor and diplomat of the Florentine Republic before the Medici restoration of 1512 cost him his office — he was arrested and tortured, then exiled to his farm outside the city. There he wrote The Prince in 1513, a short handbook on acquiring and holding power that abandoned the “mirror for princes” tradition of moral instruction, and the far longer, far more republican Discourses on Livy. His name became an adjective within a generation, which is precisely why sentences he never wrote keep arriving under it.

misattribution.heading: What's actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: This is a three-layer misattribution: the wording is unsourced, the work it gets pinned to does not contain it, and it travels in the company of an even more famous fake.

items.why: Wikiquote places it in the “Misattributed” section ↗ with a single line of comment: it is “commonly attributed to Machiavelli, which originates from an unclear source.” No earlier printing, letter or translation has been produced for it.

items.scope: The work it is pinned to
items.why: Aggregators routinely attach a book title to give the line weight — Goodreads credits it to “Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince” ↗ with no chapter or page. In the full text of Marriott’s translation ↗, the words “moral” and “morals” occur only in the translator’s introduction — not once in Machiavelli’s own text.

The two are quoted side by side constantly. Wikiquote calls it “the most common mis-quotation attributed to Machiavelli, which is never found within his works” ↗, citing Paul Rahe’s Machiavelli’s Liberal Republican Legacy.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment survives scrutiny; the sentence does not. Stanford’s Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗ states that “Machiavelli’s political theory, then, excludes issues of moral authority and legitimacy from consideration in the discussion of political decision-making and political judgment” — which is why the fake reads so convincingly. It is a fair summary wearing quotation marks it never earned.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: Machiavelli is the rare thinker whose reputation is famous enough to write quotations for him. Within a century of his death “Machiavel” was an English stage villain, and the shorthand has been generating maxims ever since — crisp, cynical, quotable sentences that sound exactly like what everyone already believes he said.

What makes this particular slogan durable is that it is not wrong about him, only wrong as a quotation. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts the scholarly reading plainly: “Machiavelli’s political theory, then, excludes issues of moral authority and legitimacy from consideration in the discussion of political decision-making and political judgment” ↗. So the eight words pass the smell test, and nobody thinks to ask for a page number.
context.detailsSummary: What he actually wrote that comes closest
detailsBody: The Prince, Chapter XV (trans. W. K. Marriott, 1908): “how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation … Hence it is necessary for a prince wishing to hold his own to know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity.”

Discourses on Livy, Book III, Chapter XLI (trans. Ninian Hill Thomson): “when the entire safety of our country is at stake, no consideration of what is just or unjust, merciful or cruel, praiseworthy or shameful, must intervene.” This is the closest Machiavelli comes to the slogan — and note that it is a tightly bounded claim about existential emergency, not a blanket divorce of politics from morality.
Both passages are argumentative and conditional. The slogan is neither. That gap is the whole story: the slogan drops the conditions and keeps the shock.
context.pull: Not wrong about him. Just not by him.
